text.p: KLM Royal Dutch Airlines surprised investors Tuesday with sharply higher-than-expected first-quarter operating profits and said its underlying performance would remain strong over the full year.

The Dutch flag carrier said operating income in its fiscal first 1997/98 quarter more than tripled to 244 million guilders ($116 million) from a year-earlier 80 million ($38 million) as burgeoning traffic revenues outstripped cost increases.

However, net profits fell to 190 million guilders ($90.5 million) from 271 million ($129 million) in the year-earlier period, when profits from the sale and revaluation of KLM's preference shares in U.S. partner Northwest Airlines inflated its bottom line by 245 million guilders ($117 million).
KLM said it expected operating profits for the full 1997/98 financial year, ending March 30, to remain strong.

The airline said traffic revenues had soared due to consistent capacity management focused on improving load factors, the proportion of seats and cargo capacity filled, and yields. Its aircraft were 4.4 percent fuller on average than a year ago, resulting in an 11 percent rise in yields, it said.
"Together with continuous cost control, this (rise in traffic revenue) has contributed to an increase in operating income of 164 million guilders ($78 million)," it said.
Currency exchange rates also helped, lifting operating income by 17 million guilders ($8 million).

Substantial book profits from KLM's 20 percent stake in Northwest Airlines have been the main factor propping up net earnings at the Dutch flag carrier in recent years as runaway costs ate into operating results. But in the latest quarter, Northwest's contribution to profits dwindled to just 56 million guilders ($27 million), a fraction of the year-earlier figure.

KLM said that unit costs rose 11 percent in the quarter, driven mainly by a higher wage bill, increased fuel costs and materials. However passenger revenues jumped 24 percent in the same period while cargo revenues rose 16 percent.
